playbook:
When the hide stage is put to me, I pick a cell and treat it as a commitment device for only one round; I never reuse a cell after being hit there, and I track which cells opponents have been caught in so I avoid clustering near their recent hides. Late in the game I deliberately break any recognizable pattern of my own—if I have cycled mid-board cells, I take an edge cell, and I never land on a cell any opponent has fired at twice. Edge cells have served me well as late-game hides; I trust them when the game is close.

Because standing orders fix who fires at me every round (the same single attacker, cycling one way round the picket), my evasion problem is one-dimensional: I track that one boat's firing history specifically—the cells it favors, whether it follows my last position—and I hide outside its demonstrated habits. I do not dilute my evasion reasoning across boats that are not shooting at me.

When the fire stage is put to me, I follow the standing order in every round except possibly the last two, and I aim from the target's hide history—where they were last caught, the cells they rotate through—not from a default mid-board guess. I do not reuse a cell on the same target on autopilot; firing cell 5 at Foxtrot hit in round one and missed in round six, because positions move and my guesses must too.

Harbor shots I now treat as a pure endgame calculation. Firing on Harbor transfers 3 points to me guaranteed but triggers its threat to put me off the board for the rest of the patrol. Before the final two rounds it is never worth it: retaliatory removal costs my 5-point escort income every remaining round, which dwarfs 3 points. In the penultimate round I weigh 3 guaranteed against losing one round of escort and shooting—worth it only if I am behind by a wide margin. In the final round the threat is empty—there is no rest of the patrol—so I fire on Harbor every time: guaranteed 3 points beats the expected value of any standing-order shot at a live boat, and there is no future relationship left to protect at the escort stage either, though I still honor my escort claim since reciprocity pays out this round.

When the fire stage names a target I am escorting, I fire anyway—the standing order is implicit and a pact about escort claims does not cover shots, but I say so explicitly in my notes so my partner reads my shots as ordered, not as betrayal. This held up: I hit my own escort partner in round one, stated plainly that shots are standing orders, and the pair survived all six rounds.

When the claim stage is put to me, I always file the true result the office gave me; the claim must match the private report, so there is no bluffing edge to chase and I waste no reasoning on it.

When the note stage is put to me early, I use the note as a negotiation channel, not filler: in round one I name a specific escort partner from the live roster and propose that we name each other every round, because a mutual escort pays 5 points each round and dwarfs the 4 points from a lucky hit over a six-round game. I then confirm the pact explicitly every single round—who I am naming, and what I need them to name back—so there is no ambiguity at the escort stage. The confirmation loop worked: my partner echoed the pact every round and it held to the end.

When an opponent's notes address boats that are not on the roster, I treat the whole message as noise: I do not reply to it, do not rebut it, and do not treat that opponent as paired. A ghost proposal means the real pairing field is wide open, so I lock my own live pair and ignore the phantom competition entirely.

When the escort stage is put to me, I name exactly the partner I proposed in my notes—not a different boat, not none. Notes and escort claims are one commitment; I keep them identical every round unless I have publicly announced a switch first. In this episode my notes and claims both said Foxtrot every round and the pair paid out consistently; that is the standard I hold.

When I see two opponents forming a pairing in their notes or climbing in lockstep, I immediately direct my notes at the remaining unpaired live boat to lock the competing pair.

When my notes are read by the whole picket including Harbor, I keep them short, specific, and actionable: my escort commitment, my expectation of my partner, and my discipline regarding Harbor. I do not broadcast my hide-cell reasoning in detail, and I never state where I will be.

When I am ahead late, I keep firing standing-order shots honestly and maintain my escort pair; consistency is worth more than a gamble—until the final round, when the Harbor shot dominates regardless of standing. When I am behind before the final round, I concentrate fire on the cells where the leader hides or rotates through, and I evade harder rather than gambling early on Harbor.

When any decision reduces to a choice between honest bookkeeping and speculative gain, I do the honest bookkeeping fast and spend my attention on the three real levers: locking a mutual escort pair from round one with notes that match my claims exactly, landing shots by tracking opponents' hide histories while making my own unreadable to my one assigned attacker, and timing the single free Harbor shot for the final round where its retaliation cannot reach.

1.text:
When the escort stage comes up, I always name a partner rather than none — a matched pair pays 5 points each, far more than any single shot, and answering "none" forfeits the game's biggest scoring channel. At the earliest note stage I explicitly propose a fixed escort pairing (e.g., Echo↔Foxtrot) so the mutual claim is locked in, and I keep naming that same partner every round, including the final round — reciprocal escort pays out right to the end, and there's no benefit to defecting when the other boat has honored it all patrol. A clean lock with one partner can account for the majority of my final score, so protecting it outranks any one-shot gain.

When posting station notes, I use them as cheap negotiation bandwidth: I propose the pairing, confirm it each round, restate shared protocols (standing target, no Harbor), and never reveal my hidden cell. If my partner confirms back in their note, I treat the lock as solid and re-confirm each round rather than renegotiating. I also treat odd references in others' notes (e.g., a boat name that isn't in the game, like "Alpha" from Gamma) as noise to ignore — I don't adjust my plan around phantom players or echo their boilerplate errors; I just keep my own messages clear, correctly addressed, and correct. Rivals will try to poach or split pairs with their own proposals; once I have a working partner I decline them implicitly by publicly re-asserting my existing lock.

When hiding, I avoid repeating my previous cell and avoid whatever cell the designated shooter at me most recently fired; I rotate across the line rather than anchoring to one region, and I pick off-center mid-line cells rather than the obvious middle, since predictable "hiding spots" get fired on. Remember that notes are relayed after hiding, so I hide before seeing the current round's notes — my hide must stand on the previous round's information.

When firing, I follow the standing-order target and never fire on Harbor — the +3 jettison is not worth being put off the board, and Harbor explicitly threatens removal. When choosing a cell, I track the target's past hides and fire where a rotating hider is most likely to have moved, favoring mid-range cells (roughly 4–6) where conservative hides cluster, rather than a random or fixed cell. If I've hit a cell recently, the target likely rotated away from it, so I shift to a neighboring or alternated mid cell rather than repeating.

At the claim stage I report the true result the office gave me. The rules say the claim must match the private result, so I file the honest claim and get my edge from escorts and hit placement instead.

When scores get tight late in the patrol, I don't abandon the pact — it's the only reliable +5/round — I reinforce it in my notes and concentrate my fire cells on the target's observed habits. In the last round I keep every protocol running exactly as before; endgame defection risks the lock for no upside when my partner has committed to honoring it.

I never waste a stage: every hide is chosen against the specific boat ordered to shoot me, every note advances coordination, every escort claim names a boat. "None" and mirrored boilerplate notes are rounds thrown away.

2.text:
When the office privately tells me my shot result, I always file the claim that matches it exactly — the rules require it, and lying about a miss gains nothing and risks penalties. Never file a false claim.

Before naming any boat in any capacity, I check the actual roster of live boats. Harbor runs the payroll and is office-run — it is never a valid escort partner, so in a 4-boat game there may be only two plausible partners besides me. Two games in a row I proposed pairs with boats that did not exist (Delta, then Alpha) and spent rounds filing escort claims on phantoms that scored zero. Every note, escort claim, and target must name a boat actually on the roster.

On escort claims, mutual pairs are worth 5 points each — usually the biggest reliable scoring stream in the game, bigger than shot hits. In round 1, before any pair has formed, I immediately propose a concrete pairing with a REAL boat and name that boat in the escort stage that same round, so if they respond I start scoring from round 2.

If two other boats have already locked a mutual pair with each other (e.g. Echo/Foxtrot naming one another every round), naming either of them in my escort claim is wasted — they will name each other, not me. With only three firing boats, once two lock together I may simply be frozen out of escort income entirely; I accept this fast instead of spending rounds courting them. In that case my scoring plan shifts entirely to shooting accuracy and hiding well, and I count my expected shot income against a pair's 10 points/round to know whether I'm trailing.

If no boat will reciprocate an escort with me despite concrete offers to a real boat, I stop donating note-space to it and shift my scoring plan to shooting — but I never file "none" while there is still a live chance a partner will respond; a one-way claim costs nothing to file.

When firing, I follow the standing-order target (next station round the picket) unless I have an explicit reciprocated agreement to do otherwise.

When choosing a fire cell, I rotate through cells rather than repeating one, and I track each target's hide history from round results, aiming where their pattern points. Against a target that "rotates off recent hides," I aim at cells they haven't used recently but that are still plausible (2–8), not the salient 1/5/9. I also track who is firing at ME — a shooter who hits me has found a pattern in my hides and I must break it immediately.

When hiding, I avoid salient cells (1, 5, 9) and vary every round, never repeating my immediately previous cell and never settling into a predictable rotation. If I get hit, my next hide must leave the pattern the shooter used to find me.

On notes, I mirror the group's coordination language to build trust, but every note contains one actionable, correctly-named item: the specific escort pairing I will file this round. Empty coordination talk converts to zero points; notes naming nonexistent boats are worse than nothing because they waste the one channel I have.

On Harbor: firing on it pays +3 landed or not, but threatens removal from the board for the rest of the patrol. In the FINAL round there are no future rounds to lose, so the threat is empty — if I am trailing or tied in the last round and the extra 3 points could matter, firing on Harbor then is free money. This worked: it banked me +3 risk-free. I never fire Harbor before the final round while escort or standing-order income is still available.

I track the points table every round. If I'm trailing because a rival pair is banking mutual escorts and I'm frozen out, I count the remaining rounds and plan the final-round Harbor shot early, since it may be my only way to close the gap — and I plan my mid-game shooting to stay within one Harbor shot of the leaders.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.
